title: Anthropic cofounder renews call for robust regulation of frontier AI
source_used: Asharq Al-Awsat, citing AFP (The Economic Times page held no text)
key_facts: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark spoke on Friday at an event at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
He said letting companies operate without robust legislation is like letting a race car loose on the streets at night without brakes.
He said the toys he buys for his children are regulated more than the super intelligence he works on.
He said US President Donald Trump, whose administration has called for the industry to police itself, was against regulation but China was not (the article attributes this to AFP).

Anthropic has been among the companies calling for governments to step in, even suggesting international coordination to slow down the whole industry, including Chinese rivals; that initiative has so far failed to materialise.
The article says a recent Anthropic report suggested small AI models may be only months away from behaving like computer worms.
quote_evidence: "It's remarkable to me that the toys I buy for my children are regulated more than the literal super intelligence I work on at my day job," he told an event at the IMF-World Bank's Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
"I think it's Formula One at night without maybe brakes in the cars," he said.
That initiative has so far failed to materialize, with companies involved in a hyper-competitive race to attract as much investment as possible.
why_it_matters_hint: A leader of a top AI lab asks governments for binding rules, at the same IMF panel where the IMF chief warned of AI risks.
notes: Economic Times page held no readable text (84 characters). Read the same story at Asharq Al-Awsat, which cites AFP for part of it; chain to the first reporter is unclear, so the entry is credited to Asharq Al-Awsat citing AFP. Reuters, via The Financial Express and BigGo Finance, also reports Clark's call for 'common sense standards' on the same panel. Overlaps with C05-02 (same panel).
